justification: Originality is strong and the central technical demonstrations are genuinely new work: the LinkRepositoryTests suite (unique-constraint rejection driving Assert.Throws<SqliteException>, real one-connection-per-test isolation), the real-vs-fake fidelity-gap program (RealLinkRepository vs. a Dictionary-backed FakeLinkRepository actually printing 'rejects' vs 'ACCEPTS' a duplicate), and the order-dependence flakiness demo (the same two checks passing or failing depending on run order against a shared connection) do not appear, in any form, in Cohn's, Fowler's or Dodds' own writing, nor in the sibling test-doubles.md article, and none of the SQL/schema/dataset choices reuse a source's running example. The balanced-view claim holds up: the article gives Cohn's economic reasoning and Google's 2015 pyramid defense equal weight with Dodds' trophy critique, states plainly that both models keep end-to-end tests thin, and locates the real disagreement (cost of the middle layer, which has fallen since 2009) rather than picking a side; its one closing heuristic (count renames-that-break-tests vs. bugs-caught) is framed as a diagnostic for over-mocked suites specifically, not a blanket argument for either shape. The EF Core SQLite-as-fake caveat is handled honestly: it is its own subsection, states the case-sensitivity and DateDiffDay gaps plainly, and explicitly does not retract the value of the integration test just demonstrated -- it reads as intellectual honesty, not self-sabotage. Exercise variety is real: classify-the-test, extend-the-repository (a genuine add-a-method-and-tests task), predict-the-match (predict-then-verify, output withheld until the solution), and find-the-bug-before-it-ships (pure reasoning, no code to run) are four distinct forms, none titled 'Predict the...' as the page's first or last exercise, and none leaks its answer outside the collapsed solution. Structure vs. the sibling test-doubles.md is clearly varied: this article uses question-form H2s throughout (a pyramid-history frame) against test-doubles' declarative/gerund headings (a five-doubles catalog frame), and it deliberately cross-links to test-doubles for AAA/double vocabulary ('Chapter 11 of Mocks, Stubs and Fakes makes the general point this test relies on...') rather than re-teaching it -- that reads as pillar coordination, not a content gap, since the prerequisite relationship is declared in front matter and the recap given (real vs. faked collaborators) is exactly the minimum this article needs and no more. No filler intro/outro, no ad code, no keyword stuffing; the toolchain sentence sits in a :::note directly before the first executed program, not as an opening provenance stamp, matching the binding rule. run-code.mjs passes clean (PASS, blocks=12, executed=6). All 13 sources are real, live pages, accurately represented in substance -- I fetched all 13 and checked the article's specific quoted and paraphrased claims against them; I found no invented facts, benchmarks or fabricated study results anywhere. Two things keep this out of pass range. First, two of the thirteen front-matter sources ('Overview - Microsoft.Data.Sqlite' and 'Getting Started with xUnit.net v3') are never cited or even alluded to in the body -- the binding pilot-round lesson makes this an automatic finding, not a style nit. Second, and more serious for an AdSense-style accuracy pass, one quotation is not what its source says: the article presents '70/20/10 split' in quotation marks as Google's testing blog's own words, but I downloaded the actual post and searched it directly -- the phrase '70/20/10' never appears in Mike Wacker's post body at all; it appears only in a reader comment, and that commenter is explicitly skeptical of it ('don't pay too much attention to 70/20/10'). The post's own text says '70% unit tests, 20% integration tests, and 10% end-to-end tests', which the article could have quoted verbatim instead. The numbers themselves are accurate and correctly sourced to the right page, so this is not an invented statistic, but wrapping a non-verbatim shorthand in quotation marks and attributing it to 'Google's own testing blog' is exactly the kind of thing a policy reviewer checking for fabricated quotes would catch, and it fails the site's own 'never fabricate ... quotes' rule as written. A second, lower-severity instance of the same problem: the Dodds quotation about component <A /> and <B /> drops 'with props c and d' and changes 'actually breaks if prop e is not supplied' to 'breaks without prop e' while still inside quotation marks -- the meaning survives but the quoted text does not match the source. Both are one-paragraph fixes; nothing here is a structural or value problem.

issues.location: "So which model should you use?" section, sentence beginning "Google's own testing blog, defending a pyramid shape in 2015, put a specific number on it: a '70/20/10 split'..."
issues.problem: '70/20/10 split' is presented in quotation marks as if it is Mike Wacker's own wording on testing.googleblog.com. It is not: I fetched the full page HTML and searched it directly. The string '70/20/10' occurs zero times in the post body; it appears twice, only in reader comments, and the one commenter who uses it is arguing against taking it too literally ('don't pay too much attention to 70/20/10 or anything like that'). The post's actual sentence is 'aim for a 70% unit tests, 20% integration tests, and 10% end-to-end tests split' (paraphrased slightly here to avoid re-quoting it verbatim in this review). The numeric split is real and correctly attributed to the right source; only the quotation-mark treatment of the shorthand is wrong.
